description: We're looking for a designer (Figma or Canva is enough) and someone who likes researching Mars and presenting. Beginners welcome, message us to join!
summary:
ARES is a browser-based mission planner for Jezero Crater, built for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. It puts NASA's orbital imagery of Mars on an interactive map in
Mars' own coordinate system, then lets anyone plan a surface traverse on top of it:
pick a preset mission or drop custom waypoints, and ARES draws the route and
reports distance, travel time, energy use and terrain alerts for an astronaut on foot or a crewed rover.
Planning a walk or a drive on Mars means weighing science targets against slopes,
sand, battery and the distance back to safety. Those trade-offs are usually hidden
inside specialist tools. ARES makes them visible in seconds, with no install and no
server. The terrain model in this prototype is simulated and labelled as such; the
imagery, coordinates and distances are real. It matters because good plans start with people who can see the ground.
details: What it does and how it works ARES has two views. The home page is a 3D Mars globe textured with NASA's Viking colour mosaic; click a named region to open a 2D map of it. The mission planner opens directly on Jezero Crater, the Perseverance landing site. In the planner you can: Read live coordinates. The cursor shows latitude and longitude to four decimals, plus modelled elevation and slope. Switch imagery. Choose between the global CTX mosaic, Viking colour and THEMIS infrared base maps, and overlay MOLA hillshade and elevation, TES albedo, USGS global geology, and the Jezero CTX (6 m/px) and HiRISE (25 cm/px) landing-site mosaics, each with its own opacity slider. Plan a mission. Start from three presets (a delta traverse, a crater-floor loop, a rim ascent) or build your own: place a lander, click to drop waypoints, drag to adjust, snap to 10 named science sites. See the consequences. The route is drawn as a polyline coloured green, amber or dashed red by terrain severity. A dashboard reports distance, travel and dwell time, energy and battery use, oxygen, climb, maximum slope and distance from the lander, with clickable alerts that fly the map to the problem. Compare vehicles. One click switches between an astronaut on foot and a crewed rover, each with its own speed, slope limits, battery and walk-back range. Export. Missions save in the browser and download as GeoJSON tagged with the Mars coordinate system. Under the hood, every route is sampled every 25 metres. At each sample the app looks up elevation, slope and hazard zones, then sums time (Tobler's hiking function for walking, a grade penalty for driving) and energy (baseline power, per-kilometre cost, and the work of climbing in Mars gravity, 3.721 m/s²). The elevation, slope and hazard data in this prototype come from a simulated terrain model shaped like Jezero (a 45 km bowl, an 80 m delta front, the Séítah sand ridges, Belva crater). They are not measured values, and the app says so on screen. Imagery, coordinates and distances are real. Page 4 of 8 ARES – NASA Space Apps 2026 submission pack Benefits and intended impact For EVA and rover planning: it shows in one screen the trade-off planners care about: which science stops fit inside slope limits, battery, an 8-hour sortie and a walk-back radius. The same route can be safe on foot and a no-go on wheels, and ARES shows that in one click. For students and the public: it turns NASA's Mars imagery into something you can plan on, with real place names from the Perseverance mission and no software to install. For future work: the terrain model sits behind one function. Replacing it with a real elevation model upgrades every slope, energy and alert calculation without touching the rest of the app. What we hope to achieve next: connect a real Jezero elevation model, add automatic routing around hazards, and extend beyond Jezero to other candidate landing sites.
